# Sharp projective energy versus a containing-cap fraction

Let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, d≥1, let y∈int K, and write V=|K|. Its projective energy is

    E_K(y)=min_a ∫_K [1+a·(x−y)]^(−d−1) dx,

with the affine denominator positive on all of K. Attainment and strict parameter convexity were proved in `candidate 5811f0ad1132ce56`.

Put Γ_d=(d/(d+1))^d and define, on 0≤α≤Γ_d,

    F_d(α)=((d+1)^(d+1)/d^d) α(1−α^(1/d)).           (1)

**Theorem.** If ANY halfspace through y captures volume αV with 0<α≤Γ_d, then

    E_K(y)/V ≤ F_d(α).                                (2)

The cap need not be globally minimal. In particular, if α is the ordinary halfspace depth fraction at y, then (2) applies when α≤Γ_d. When α>Γ_d one retains E_K(y)≤V.

The proof is a direct comparison of actual parallel sections with a finite cone. It does not use localization, a conjectural density theorem, or an assumed minimum-cap classification. The cone-comparison mechanism was proposed by root and independently derived here, including support-endpoint and equality details.

## 1. A finite cone with the same two half-masses

Assume d≥2, translate y to zero, and write the chosen cap as t=u·x≥0 with |u|=1. Let f(t) be the (d−1)-volume of the actual section K∩{u·x=t}; thus ∫f=V. Its support is a finite interval [A,B], with A<0<B and f(0)=f_0>0. On its open support, f^(1/(d−1)) is concave by convexity and Brunn–Minkowski. Extend f by zero outside [A,B]; endpoint values do not affect any integral.

Define

    b=dαV/f_0,
    r=α^(1/d),
    a=b(1−1/r)<0,
    ψ(t)=f_0(1−t/b)^(d−1)  for a≤t≤b,
         0 otherwise.                                (3)

Then ψ(0)=f_0, ∫_0^b ψ=αV and ∫_a^0 ψ=(1−α)V. In particular its total mass is V.

The actual positive support endpoint satisfies B≤b. Indeed, select a highest point of K at height B. The convex hull of that point and the section at height zero lies in K. Its sections at height t∈[0,B] have (d−1)-volume f_0(1−t/B)^(d−1). Integration gives

    αV=∫_0^B f(t)dt ≥ f_0B/d.

This uses the actual 0-section and works even when the top supporting face is not a point.

## 2. Two one-crossing comparisons

Let ψ_∞(t)=f_0(1−t/b)^(d−1) for t≤b, without the lower truncation. On the actual projection interval put

    q(t)=f(t)^(1/(d−1))−f_0^(1/(d−1))(1−t/b).

The function q is concave and q(0)=0. Consequently q(t)/t is nonincreasing for positive t. Since B≤b and the positive masses of f and ψ agree, exactly one of the following holds:

* f=ψ almost everywhere on [0,b]; or
* f−ψ has signs positive then negative on (0,b), with zeros allowed.

For precision, if q is never positive on (0,B), the matched masses force the first case. Otherwise its positive set starts at zero and is an interval, by concavity with q(0)=0; it can change to nonpositive only once. Beyond B the difference is nonpositive. An actual nonzero facet value at B can create a downward jump to zero there; this is compatible with, and does not reverse, the asserted sign pattern. Matching the positive masses then forces a nontrivial negative part as well.

The same concavity gives

    f(t)≤ψ_∞(t) for EVERY negative t, up to endpoint values. (4)

If q(s)>0 for some s>0, apply concavity at 0 between any t<0 and s: it forces q(t)<0. In the equality case on the positive side, q(s)=q(0)=0 for interior positive s, and the same inequality gives q(t)≤0. Outside the actual support f=0, so (4) remains valid.

Now compare the negative restrictions of f and the TRUNCATED ψ from (3). On t<a their difference is nonnegative, while on a<t<0 it is nonpositive by (4). Their negative masses match. Thus this difference also has the signs positive then negative.

The elementary one-crossing rule says: if two integrable densities of the same mass have difference nonnegative before one point and nonpositive after it, then

    ∫ w f ≤ ∫ w ψ                                    (5)

for every increasing function w for which the integrals exist. Subtract its value at the crossing point and integrate the pointwise sign inequality. Applying this rule separately on the positive and negative half-lines proves (5) for the complete section laws here. If w is strictly increasing, equality requires the two laws to coincide almost everywhere.

Equivalently, both restricted actual laws are stochastically below their matched cone laws. In particular the argument permits the actual body to extend farther in the negative direction than the comparison cone.

## 3. The admissible increasing projective kernel

Put N=d+1. The one-coordinate energy optimizer for ψ is

    c=(Nr−d)/[N b(1−r)]≤0.                            (6)

Its endpoint denominators are

    1+cb=1/[N(1−r)]>0,
    1+ca=d/(Nr)>0.                                    (7)

Since B≤b and c≤0, 1+ct is positive on ALL of the actual support [A,B], even if A<a. Thus a physical parameter c u is admissible in the full energy minimization of K. Its kernel

    w(t)=(1+ct)^(−N)

is increasing, strictly so when α<Γ_d. The one-crossing comparison therefore gives

    E_K(0) ≤ ∫ f(t)w(t)dt ≤ ∫ ψ(t)w(t)dt.             (8)

We evaluate the last quantity exactly. Under ψ/V, the variable s=(b−t)/(b−a) has density d s^(d−1) on [0,1]. For arbitrary positive endpoint denominators L_b=1+cb and L_a=1+ca,

    ∫_0^1 d s^(d−1)[L_b+(L_a−L_b)s]^(−d−1)ds
       =1/(L_b L_a^d).                               (9)

Differentiate s^d/[L_b(L_b+(L_a−L_b)s)^d] to verify (9). Equivalently the one-direction objective is V/[(1+cb)(1+ca)^d]; differentiating it shows that (6) is its unique minimizer, including c=0 at r=d/(d+1). Substituting (7) into (9) gives

    ∫ψ w =V N^(d+1)r^d(1−r)/d^d=V F_d(α).

This proves (2) without a tangent-centroid assumption on the original section at y. When α=Γ_d, c=0 and the bound is simply E≤V.

## 4. Intervals, equality and exact sharpness

For d=1, write K=[−l,r] about y=0, with l,r>0. Its energy is 4lr/(l+r). If a through-point cap has fraction α≤1/2, then α=min(l,r)/(l+r), and

    E_K(0)/V=4α(1−α),

exactly (1). This treats the dimension omitted by the section-root argument.

For d≥2 and α<Γ_d, equality in (8) requires f=ψ almost everywhere, because its kernel is strictly increasing. This exact section profile forces K to be a cone over a full (d−1)-dimensional base in t=a, with one apex in t=b. Here are the geometric details. Convex-body sections converge in Hausdorff distance to the endpoint section as t approaches a from above: upper convergence is compactness, and lower convergence follows by interpolating the endpoint section with any fixed interior point. Thus the base section has the required positive endpoint volume. Fix a top point. Its cone over this base is contained in K and has exactly the same section volume at every interior height. The included convex sections with equal positive volume are equal. Closure identifies the whole body and forces the top section to be that single point.

Equality in the FIRST step of (8) further requires that c u be the full projective optimizer. In a cone the section centroids are affine in t. The vertical stationarity of (6) makes the corresponding weighted mean height zero; horizontal stationarity therefore holds exactly when y is the centroid of its parallel section, that is, when y lies on the segment joining the apex to the base centroid. This condition is also sufficient. Thus for α<Γ_d the equality bodies/marks are precisely these cones with the indicated axial mark and cap toward the apex, up to affine changes of coordinates. At α=Γ_d, equality E=V is exactly the ordinary-centroid condition; no separate Grünbaum equality classification is needed for the theorem.

In particular, choose ANY convex (d−1)-base with centroid zero, an apex above it, and an axial mark for which the fraction toward the apex is α=r^d with 0<r≤d/(d+1). The full energy equals V F_d(α) by the just-verified stationarity. This cap is GLOBALLY minimal: if another containing cap had fraction β<α, it would satisfy β<Γ_d and (2) would give

    E/V≤F_d(β)<F_d(α),

a contradiction. The strict increase used here is proved in the next section. This certifies sharpness and global cap minimality together, rather than presuming a vertex-direction cap is minimal.

For the standard simplex and y=(ε,...,ε), 0<ε≤1/(d+1), the axial cap toward the origin has α=(dε)^d. Its energy is V(d+1)^(d+1)(1−dε)ε^d, recovering the proposed calibration with globally certified minimum depth.

## 5. Quantitative lower bounds on the actual ordinary depth

Let α_K(y) be the minimum containing-halfspace fraction. This minimum is attained over through-point unit normals: cap mass is continuous there, and the sphere is compact. The point is interior, so all those masses are positive. Any containing halfspace can be tightened to one through the point without increasing mass.

On [0,Γ_d], F_d is continuous, strictly increasing, and maps the endpoints to 0 and 1. Indeed

    F_d'(α)=((d+1)^(d+1)/d^d)
                       [1−((d+1)/d)α^(1/d)].

The theorem and the trivial case α_K>Γ_d give the universal ordinary bound

    α_K(y) ≥ F_d^(−1)(E_K(y)/V).                      (10)

It is sharp at every energy ratio in (0,1] by the cones of Section 4.

A closed-form weaker consequence follows from

    −F_d''(Γ_d)=((d+1)/d)^(2d+1)=c_d,
    −F_d''(α)≥c_d for 0<α≤Γ_d.

Since F_d(Γ_d)=1 and F_d'(Γ_d)=0, integration gives

    F_d(α)≤1−(c_d/2)(Γ_d−α)².

Consequently

    α_K(y) ≥ Γ_d max{0,
          1−sqrt[(2d/(d+1))(1−E_K(y)/V)]}.            (11)

For d=1 this is the exact interval formula. For d>1, (10) is the exact sharper inverse bound; (11) is a convenient elementary estimate.

The invariant and both conversions are ordinary fiber statements. Joint Minkowski concavity of E may supply a valid energy lower bound in an actual compatible fiber family, after which (10) converts that bound to own-fiber depth. No sum of such own depths, lattice-preserving localization, cap-menu allocation, or mixed OC conclusion is inferred here.
